laws.name: Criminal Code, general production order
laws.text: A judge or justice of the peace can order a person or company to produce documents or data in its possession or control, when there are reasonable grounds to believe they will be evidence of an offence.
laws.short: A judge in Canada can order a company to hand over data it holds that may be evidence of an offence.

laws.name: Criminal Code, production order for transmission data
laws.text: A judge or justice of the peace can order a person or company to produce transmission data in its possession or control: when, how long and between whom communications happened, but not what they said. It takes reasonable grounds to suspect the data will help investigate an offence.
laws.short: A Canadian judge can order a company to reveal when, how long and with whom you communicated, but not what you said.

laws.name: National Intelligence Law, Articles 7 and 14
laws.citation: National Intelligence Law of the People's Republic of China (2017, amended 2018), arts. 7 and 14
laws.text: Requires all organizations and citizens to support, assist and cooperate with national intelligence work in accordance with law, and to keep confidential any secrets of that work they become aware of. Intelligence agencies can ask them for that support.
laws.short: Chinese law requires every organization and citizen to support state intelligence work and keep its secrets.

laws.name: Code of Criminal Procedure, section 95 (duty to hand over)
laws.text: Requires anyone holding an object that may matter as evidence to produce it and hand it over on demand. Refusing can bring fines and coercive detention, except for people entitled to refuse to testify.
laws.short: In Germany, anyone holding something that may be evidence must hand it over on demand, or face fines and detention.

laws.text: For serious crimes, and some crimes committed online, a court, or a prosecutor in urgent cases, can order a provider of digital services to hand over users' usage data, location data included. The provider must give the information without delay.

laws.name: e-Evidence Regulation (European Production Orders)
laws.text: An authority in one EU country can order an online service based in another to hand over user data in 10 days, or 8 hours in an emergency. Account details need a prosecutor's order; content, or who contacted whom and when, needs a judge and usually a crime carrying three years or more in prison.
laws.short: An EU authority can order a company in another EU country to hand over data, sometimes within hours.

status_note.text: Applies from 2026-08-18. It covers orders from one EU country to a provider established or represented in another; a country's own powers over providers based there are national law, which FinePrint hasn't reviewed yet. The provider must keep the order confidential; the issuing authority tells the person, unless national law lets it delay or skip that (art. 13).

laws.text: The central or a state government can order an agency to intercept, monitor or decrypt any information in a computer, for national security, public order or investigating any offence. laws.name: Criminal Procedure Act, section 210 (production order)
laws.text: A court can order whoever holds something likely to matter as evidence, electronically stored data included, to hand it over if they would have to testify in the case. If waiting would harm the investigation, the prosecution can order it first, for a court to approve as soon as possible.
laws.short: A Norwegian court can order anyone holding evidence, data included, to hand it over; prosecutors can order it first in urgent cases.

laws.name: Federal Law No. 149-FZ on Information, Article 10.1
laws.citation: Federal Law of 27 July 2006 No. 149-FZ, art. 10.1, parts 1, 3, 3.1 and 4.1 (consolidated through No. 210-FZ of 26 June 2026)
laws.text: Requires internet services that handle users' messages to store, in Russia, data about those communications and users for three years and the messages for up to six months; to give them to the authorities in cases set by federal law; and to give the security service what it needs to decrypt them.
laws.short: Russia requires messaging services to store user data in Russia, hand it to the authorities when federal law says so, and help decrypt it.

laws.citation: Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (2020 Rev. Ed.), s. 20(1) and (1A)
laws.text: A police officer of sergeant rank or above can issue a written order requiring anyone believed to hold a document, thing or data, or able to reach it from a computer, to produce it or a copy, or give access, when the officer considers it necessary or desirable for an investigation or trial.
laws.short: A Singapore police officer can order anyone holding documents or data, or able to reach them from a computer, to produce them.

laws.name: CLOUD Act
laws.text: Requires providers of communication and cloud services to disclose data in their possession, custody or control under US legal process, whether it is stored in the United States or elsewhere.
laws.short: US legal process can make a provider hand over data it holds, even data stored outside the United States.

laws.name: FISA Section 702
laws.text: Section 702 let the government direct providers to hand over communications of foreign targets abroad. It was repealed on 2026-06-12; directives issued before then stay in force until they expire, and the FISA court can order a provider to comply. The last certification reportedly runs into 2027.
laws.short: Section 702 was repealed on 2026-06-12, but directives already issued to providers stay in force until they expire.

status_note.text: Repealed when its last extension ran out (Pub. L. 119-87). Lawmakers have said the FISA court approved the last certification in March 2026, for up to a year, so it ends by March 2027 at the latest; after that, surveillance needs individual FISA Title I orders. A directive itself requires the provider to keep the surveillance secret: automatic (§ 1881a(i)(1)(A)).
